meta.title: Turkish C1
meta.subtitle: 997 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Turkish → English (see the Turkish, recall the meaning) and English → Turkish (see an English meaning, recall the Turkish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 997 words for level C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: the Yunus Emre Institute's Turkish Proficiency Exam (TYS) certifies only B2 and C1 and publishes no vocabulary list. The scope of this deck is taken instead from the Turkish as a Foreign Language Teaching Programme (Türkçenin Yabancı Dil Olarak Öğretimi Programı; Türkiye Maarif Foundation, 2nd edition, 2020, approved by Turkey's Ministry of National Education), a CEFR-based syllabus whose C1 tables for secondary school (pp. 295–304) are organised in ten themes: communication, education and learning to learn, health, youth, travel and migration between countries, global warming, the economy past and present, science and technology, between cultures, and the language of art. FROM A2 UP THE PROGRAMME LISTS NO VOCABULARY AT ALL: its A2 table says the vocabulary section was left out so as not to limit the level, and the C1 tables carry none either. What each theme gives instead is its suggested topics — body language and communication breakdowns, kinds of education and exam anxiety, alternative medicine, stress and psychology, the generation gap and popular culture, migration and its law, water resources and extinction, finance, trade routes and global capital, genetics, data security and the ethics of science, cultural interaction and diversity, artists, poetry and the stage. So 95 of the 997 words were written for Folio for those topics, a theme at a time, and are Folio's choice rather than the programme's. This is not an official word list and is not presented as one. No word taught in the levels below is repeated. The other 902 are the commonest words of everyday Turkish, from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles. The cards are ordered by that frequency, so the words met most often come first; the 5 two-word expressions, which a list of single words cannot count, come last. Turkish builds words by adding suffixes, and a suffix's vowel follows the vowels of the word (vowel harmony) while some stems change before it, so the card carries the forms that cannot be guessed, read from a dictionary rather than generated. 544 nouns show their plural and five cases — bulaşık: bulaşıklar, bulaşığı, bulaşığa, bulaşıkta, bulaşıktan, bulaşığın. 101 verbs show the third person of the present, the aorist (the general present), the past and the future — kutsamak: kutsuyor, kutsar, kutsadı, kutsayacak — the aorist's vowel being the one a learner cannot predict. Adjectives do not inflect and carry no forms. Real example sentences come with 979 of the 997 words, three apiece for 936, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Scope: Türkçenin Yabancı Dil Olarak Öğretimi Programı, Türkiye Maarif Vakfı, 2020 (ISBN 978-605-80438-2-4). Meanings, forms and parts of speech: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
